stem: A 70-year-old woman who travels between seasonal work sites presents after more than three months of right-sided chest discomfort and progressive breathlessness, which the group attributed to 'the change in climate' at her most recent work site. She only agreed to be seen when she became too breathless to continue working. She has had low-grade fevers she hadn't mentioned. No prior TB treatment, no known TB contact, no known drug-resistant contact. Chest imaging and exam reveal a large right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis was performed; pleural fluid was sent for molecular testing (along with biochemical and ADA testing), which returned positive for M. tuberculosis. Exam: decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right base, no peripheral edema, no lymphadenopathy.

patient.social_history: Travels between seasonal work sites with extended family; symptoms initially attributed to a change in climate
patient.presenting_complaint: Right-sided chest discomfort and progressive breathlessness, low-grade fevers
patient.exam_findings: Decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at right base, no peripheral edema, no lymphadenopathy, large right pleural effusion on imaging
patient.prior_treatment: None for this episode; no prior TB treatment ever

distractors: A change in climate at her work site proposed as sufficient explanation for the chest discomfort and breathlessness
Age-related decline in exercise tolerance proposed as an alternative to a new pulmonary or pleural process
A viral or bacterial pleuritic illness assumed self-limited, delaying pursuit of thoracentesis
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the pleural fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the pleural fluid), alongside biochemical/ADA testing, as a first-line microbiological tool rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology alone.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the pleural effusion entirely to environmental/climate conditions and deferring molecular testing on the pleural fluid already obtained
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
